stories.title: The Woman at the Well
stories.passageSummary: Jesus comes to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Jacob's well is there. Jesus, wearied with his journey, sits on the well. It is about the sixth hour. There comes a woman of Samaria to draw water. Jesus says: Give me to drink. His disciples have gone away into the city to buy food. The woman says: How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, who am a woman of Samaria? — for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. Jesus answers: If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that says to thee, Give me to drink, thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water. She says: Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: whence then hast thou that living water? Art thou greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well? Jesus answers: Whosoever drinks of this water shall thirst again, but whosoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up unto everlasting life. The woman says: Sir, give me this water, that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw. Jesus says: Go, call thy husband, and come hither. She answers: I have no husband. Jesus says: Thou hast well said, I have no husband; for thou hast had five husbands, and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly. The woman says: Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet. Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship. Jesus says: Woman, believe me, the hour cometh when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father. Ye worship ye know not what; we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews. But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth. The woman says: I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things. Jesus says: I that speak unto thee am he.

stories.title: Five Loaves and Two Fish
stories.passageSummary: The apostles gather together unto Jesus and tell him all things, both what they have done, and what they have taught. Jesus says: Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while — for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat. They depart into a desert place by ship privately. The people see them departing, and many know him, and run afoot thither out of all cities, and outgo them, and come together unto him. Jesus, when he comes out, sees much people, and is moved with compassion toward them, because they are as sheep not having a shepherd: and he begins to teach them many things. When the day is now far spent, his disciples come unto him, and say: This is a desert place, and now the time is far passed; send them away, that they may go into the country round about, and into the villages, and buy themselves bread; for they have nothing to eat. Jesus answers: Give ye them to eat. They say: Shall we go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread, and give them to eat? Jesus says: How many loaves have ye? Go and see. When they know, they say: Five, and two fishes. He commands them to make all sit down by companies upon the green grass. They sit down in ranks, by hundreds, and by fifties. And when he has taken the five loaves and the two fishes, he looks up to heaven, and blesses, and breaks the loaves, and gives them to his disciples to set before them; and the two fishes divides he among them all. They all eat, and are filled. They take up twelve baskets full of the fragments, and of the fishes. And they that ate of the loaves were about five thousand men.

stories.title: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
stories.passageSummary: Jesus speaks this parable unto certain which trust in themselves that they are righteous, and despise others. Two men go up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stands and prays thus with himself: God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, will not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smites upon his breast, saying: God be merciful to me a sinner. Jesus says: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

stories.title: More Than Conquerors
stories.passageSummary: What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us? He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written: For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. This is Paul writing to the church at Rome — an exultation, not a narrative. Render the scene as Paul dictating to a scribe, the words coming with mounting cadence, the question-and-answer rhythm building. Or render the words landing in a small house church where the letter is being read aloud for the first time. Either framing keeps the passage as observable scene rather than abstract argument.

stories.title: So Great a Cloud of Witnesses
stories.passageSummary: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. This is the writer of Hebrews addressing weary believers — a benediction-like exhortation, not a Bible narrative scene. Render the passage as words being read aloud or preached in a gathering of weary believers, the cloud-of-witnesses image taking shape in their minds, the race image taking shape in the room. Or render the writer dictating, the cadence of the three verses unfolding. Keep it observable scene rather than abstract exhortation.
